subject: Mathematics
title: Real Numbers and Approximation
learningOutcomes: Classify numbers into the sets of natural, whole, integer, rational and irrational numbers and understand how each set sits inside the next.
Identify terminating, recurring and non-terminating non-recurring decimals and connect them to rational and irrational numbers.
Recognise proper, improper, mixed and unit fractions and carry out the four operations on fractions and mixed numbers, keeping track of signs.
Round whole numbers and decimals to a given number of decimal places, to the nearest 10/100/1000, and to a given number of significant figures.
Distinguish rounding from truncation and explain rounding and truncation errors.
Estimate the results of calculations by rounding to 1 or 2 significant figures and use estimation to check answers and compare value for money.

sections.heading: The Sets of Numbers
sections.body: Numbers are grouped into sets, and each set sits inside the next larger one. Natural numbers \(\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, ...\}\) are the counting numbers. Adding zero gives the whole numbers \(\mathbb{W} = \{0, 1, 2, 3, ...\}\). Adding negatives gives the integers \(\mathbb{Z} = \{..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...\}\). A rational number \(\mathbb{Q}\) is any number that can be written as a ratio \(\frac{a}{b}\) of two integers with \(b \neq 0\) — every integer is rational because \(n = \frac{n}{1}\). Numbers that cannot be written as such a fraction, like \(\pi\) and \(\sqrt{2}\), are irrational. Together the rationals and irrationals make up the real numbers, so \(\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}\).

sections.heading: Decimals and Fractions
sections.body: A rational number written as a decimal is either terminating (the digits end, e.g. \(0.75\)) or non-terminating recurring (a digit or group repeats forever, e.g. \(\frac{1}{3} = 0.\overline{3}\)). A non-terminating, non-recurring decimal never ends and never repeats — these are the irrational numbers such as \(\pi\) and \(\sqrt{2}\). Fractions come in types too: a proper fraction has numerator smaller than denominator; an improper fraction has numerator greater than or equal to the denominator; a mixed number is a whole number plus a proper fraction; and a unit fraction is a proper fraction with numerator 1. Final answers are usually written as mixed numbers, and to divide by a fraction you multiply by its reciprocal — the reciprocal of \(\frac{a}{b}\) is \(\frac{b}{a}\).

sections.heading: Rounding Off
sections.body: To round a number, look at the digit immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up (add 1 to the kept digit); if it is less than 5, keep the digit the same. Digits before the decimal point are replaced with zeros as place-holders, and digits after it are dropped. A key rule: never round twice. Always work from the original number straight to the required accuracy — to round \(96.482\) to a whole number, use \(96.482\) directly, not \(96.5\). Trailing zeros matter for showing accuracy: \(8.40\) tells the reader the value is correct to two decimal places, so it is not simply written as \(8.4\).

sections.heading: Significant Figures
sections.body: Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning and show a number's precision; the more significant figures given, the more accurate the number. The rules are: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; trailing zeros in the decimal part are significant; leading zeros before the first non-zero digit are just place-holders and are not significant; and trailing zeros in a whole number may or may not be significant depending on how the number was approximated. So \(3068\) has 4 significant figures, \(0.00620\) has 3, and \(0.0082\) has 2. To round to a number of significant figures, use the same 5-or-more round-up rule on the digit after the last figure you keep.

sections.heading: Rounding vs Truncation and Their Errors
sections.body: Truncation (chopping) simply cuts off all digits after the required position without looking at the next digit, so for a positive number it always rounds down towards zero. This is why \(\sqrt{162} = 12.727...\) rounds to \(12.728\) but truncates to \(12.727\). Rounding at intermediate steps introduces a rounding error, and truncating introduces a truncation error. To keep a final answer accurate to \(n\) significant figures, carry at least \(n+1\) significant figures through the intermediate working, and only round the very last result.

sections.heading: Estimation
sections.body: Estimation finds an approximate value using rough or convenient numbers, and is used when the exact value is not needed or is impractical to find. To estimate a calculation, round each number to 1 or 2 significant figures and work it out mentally — for example \(798 \times 195 \approx 800 \times 200 = 160000\). Estimation is the quickest way to check whether a calculator answer is reasonable. For value-for-money problems, find the cost per unit (per gram, per millilitre) of each option and compare; the smaller unit cost is the better value.

definitions.definition: A number that can be written as a ratio of two integers \(\frac{a}{b}\) with \(b \neq 0\).
A number that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers; its decimal never ends and never repeats.
A whole number or its negative: \(..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...\)
A decimal whose digits end after a finite number of places.
A decimal that never ends but repeats a digit or group of digits forever.
The fraction turned upside down; the reciprocal of \(\frac{a}{b}\) is \(\frac{b}{a}\).
The digits in a number that carry meaning and show how precise it is.
Chopping off the digits after a chosen position without rounding.
Finding an approximate value using rough or convenient numbers.

examTips: Zero is a whole number but NOT a natural number — natural numbers start at 1.
A terminating decimal and a recurring decimal are both rational; only a non-terminating, non-recurring decimal (like \(\pi\) or \(\sqrt{2}\)) is irrational.
Never round twice. Round the original number straight to the required accuracy — don't round to 1 d.p. first and then to a whole number.
Leading zeros are never significant (\(0.0082\) has 2 s.f.); zeros between non-zero digits always are (\(3068\) has 4 s.f.).
Truncation always chops downward, so a truncation error is usually smaller than or equal to the matching rounding error.
When estimating, round each number to 1 or 2 significant figures first, then use the estimate only to check that your exact answer is reasonable.
